passages.happening:
Eliphaz goes on. “Call out if you please, but who will answer? To which of the holy ones will you turn?” (verse 1).

Resentment kills a fool, he says. He has seen a fool take root, and then his house was cursed, his sons crushed in court with no one to defend them, his harvest eaten by the hungry.

“For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground. Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Eliphaz's first question assumes there are heavenly beings who might plead for a person before God. His point is that none will help Job if Job is in the wrong. Later Job will long for exactly such a go-between (9:33; 16:19).

In court in verse 4 is literally in the gate, where a town's elders sat to settle disputes. To be crushed there without a defender meant losing one's case with no one to speak for you.

The proverb of verse 7 uses an image from daily life, sparks rising from a fire. The Hebrew says the sons of Resheph fly upward. Resheph was the name of a Canaanite god of plague and fire, but here the word is used as a poet's word for flames, much as English uses old names in ordinary speech. Trouble, amal, is the word Job used in 3:10. Eliphaz means that trouble is the human lot, and that it does not come from nowhere.

The picture of the fool whose sons are crushed and whose house is cursed is a hard thing to say to a man whose children have just died. Eliphaz may not mean it of Job. But Job will hear it.
passages.later: The word for trouble runs through Ecclesiastes, where the Teacher looks at all the toil of life: ‘What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?’ (Ecclesiastes 1:3).
passages.asks: Eliphaz spoke about the fool's children to a man who had just buried his own. Ask whether your words, however true, have landed on someone's fresh wound. And ask how you could listen first, and speak later.

passages.t: Appeal to the God who does great things
passages.happening:
“However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him” (verse 8). Eliphaz turns to praise of God, ‘the One who does great and unsearchable things, wonders without number’ (verse 9).

God gives rain to the earth and water to the fields. He sets the lowly on high and lifts mourners to safety. He frustrates the plans of the crafty. “He catches the wise in their craftiness, and sweeps away the plans of the cunning” (verse 13). He saves the needy from the powerful. “So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This is the heart of Eliphaz's counsel, and much of it could stand in the Psalms. It follows the pattern of a hymn, describing what God does: he gives rain, lifts the lowly, thwarts the crafty and saves the needy. These are true descriptions of God, found throughout Scripture.

Eliphaz's advice is good advice in general: bring your case to God. Job will do exactly that, more boldly than Eliphaz imagines, and he will not be talked out of it.

The friends' words can hold real wisdom even where their use of it against Job is wrong, and that is part of what makes the book demanding to read.
passages.later: Paul writes that ‘the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight’ (1 Corinthians 3:19), and he quotes verse 13 to prove it: God's wisdom, shown in the message of the cross, overturns human cleverness. And a psalm says nearly what verse 16 says: “The upright see and rejoice, and all iniquity shuts its mouth” (Psalm 107:42).
passages.asks: Eliphaz praised a God who lifts mourners to safety. Ask whether you believe that of God for yourself, or only for others. And ask whom you know who needs someone to bring their case to God for them.

passages.happening:
“Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty. For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal” (verses 17-18).

Eliphaz piles up promises. God will rescue Job from six troubles, and in seven no harm will touch him. In famine he will be redeemed from death, and in battle from the sword. He will laugh at destruction. He will be in covenant with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with him. His tent will be secure, his descendants many, and he will come to the grave ‘in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season’ (verse 26).

“Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The idea of discipline comes from the family. A father corrects a son he loves, and the wisdom tradition applied this to God's dealings with his people. Eliphaz calls Job's suffering the discipline, musar, of the Almighty. Shaddai, the Almighty, is one of the oldest names for God, used with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and it appears more often in Job than in any other book.

Six troubles, and in seven none, is a Hebrew way of saying a full number of troubles. The promises describe what every family in that world hoped for: a safe tent, many children, a long life. They also list what Job has already lost.

Eliphaz ends with the confidence of a man who has checked his work. That confidence is exactly what the book calls into question.
passages.later: Proverbs says something very like verse 17: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the LORD, and do not loathe His rebuke; for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:11-12).
passages.hard:
Is suffering God's discipline?

Scripture does teach that God disciplines his children, as a father corrects a son he loves (Proverbs 3:11-12), and many believers have looked back on hard years and seen that God taught them something there. Eliphaz is not wrong that this can happen.

But the book of Job shows that not all suffering is discipline for sin. The reader knows that Job's suffering is not, because God has said so twice. Eliphaz could not see that, and he spoke as if he could. He promised that no harm would touch a man whose ten children had just died.

No one may tell a person in pain that their suffering is God's correction, as if they could read God's reasons from the outside. The book calls that speaking wrongly of God (42:7). Whatever God may be doing in someone's life, it is not for anyone else to announce.
passages.asks: Eliphaz offered Job a cure for a sickness Job did not have. Ask whether someone has ever explained your trouble in a way that did not fit. And ask how you might speak to a friend in trouble without claiming to know why it came.
